text: Not every 2 by 2 matrix of numbers is a valid quantum gate, and not every Hermitian-looking matrix actually is Hermitian. This lesson turns the two defining properties of quantum gates and observables into a few lines of NumPy you can run against any matrix.

Unitary asks whether a matrix preserves length: U at-sign U dot conj dot T must equal the identity matrix. Every valid quantum gate must be unitary. Hermitian asks a different question, whether a matrix equals its own conjugate transpose, and Hermitian matrices represent observables, not gates. Pauli-Y turns out to satisfy both definitions at once, while the S-gate proves the two properties are genuinely independent.

Rather than eyeballing printed matrices, wrap both checks into reusable functions using np dot allclose instead of exact equality. is_unitary multiplies U by its conjugate transpose and compares to the identity. is_hermitian compares A directly to its own conjugate transpose. Eight lines, and they're exactly what gets reused in Lesson 13's lab and every later gate-building exercise.

Running both checks on Pauli-Y returns True and True, it's genuinely both unitary and Hermitian. Running them on the S-gate, diagonal one and j, returns True for unitary but False for Hermitian, because S has j in its bottom-right corner while its conjugate transpose has negative j there. S is a perfectly legal quantum gate, but it doesn't correspond to a measurable physical observable the way a Hermitian matrix would.

Next lesson explains why every one of these allclose checks matters in the first place: the floating-point reality that makes exact equality the wrong tool for comparing any computed probability, norm, or matrix product.
